title: Transistor Switch Explorer
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Robotics and Computational Thinking
description: An N-channel MOSFET circuit in which an RP2040 GPIO pin drives the gate through a 220 ohm resistor and the MOSFET switches a DC motor powered by a 6 V battery pack. Meters compare the tiny GPIO current with the large motor current, and a direct-connection option shows why a GPIO pin cannot power a motor.

educational.topic: Transistors as electronic switches for motor control
learningObjectives: Explain how a small voltage on a MOSFET's gate switches a large current from drain to source.
Identify the gate threshold voltage at which the motor starts to turn.
Compare the GPIO control current with the motor current and describe their ratio.
Explain why a DC motor cannot be powered directly from a GPIO pin.
prerequisites: Voltage and current as basic ideas
Motors need more power than LEDs

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Guided exploration of a simplified circuit model with numeric meters
pedagogical.interactionPattern: Students toggle the GPIO pin or drag the gate voltage slider, change the motor load, and bypass the transistor while meters and a ratio line update.
keyQuestions: At what gate voltage does the MOSFET turn on?
Where does the motor current come from: the GPIO pin or the battery?
About how many times larger is the motor current than the GPIO current?
What happens when the motor is wired straight to the GPIO pin?
commonMisconceptions: The motor current flows out of the GPIO pin.
Any voltage above 0 V on the gate turns the transistor fully on.
A GPIO pin can power a small motor if the program sets it HIGH.
The transistor creates the extra current, instead of switching current that comes from the battery.
assessmentOpportunities: Record the threshold voltage found with the slider.
Challenge: explain why the direct GPIO connection fails.
Exit ticket: label gate, drain, and source and trace the motor current path.
